questions.question: What does the `fr` unit in `grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr` represent?
options: A fraction of the remaining space after fixed-size tracks are laid out, so the second column gets twice the leftover space of the first
A percentage of the viewport width
The number of grid items allowed in that column
questions.explanation: fr units divide up whatever space is left over once any fixed-width tracks (like 240px) are accounted for.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of `grid-template-areas` over positioning items with numeric `grid-column`/`grid-row` values?
options: It renders faster in the browser
The template string visually maps out the layout, making the structure self-documenting and easier to read at a glance
It's required for responsive design to work
questions.explanation: A named grid-template-areas string literally looks like the layout, which is easier for a reader to parse than tracking numeric line positions.

questions.question: What does `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr))` achieve without any media queries?
options: A fixed 3-column layout on all screen sizes
As many 240px-minimum columns as fit the container, stretched evenly to fill leftover space, automatically dropping columns as the container narrows
A single column on every screen size
It has no effect without an explicit column count
questions.explanation: auto-fit with minmax lets the browser calculate how many columns fit at the minimum size and stretch them to fill the rest — a fully responsive grid with zero breakpoints.

questions.question: According to general guidance, when should you reach for Grid instead of Flexbox?
options: Never — Flexbox can always do everything Grid can
When rows and columns both need to align together, such as a dashboard or card gallery, versus Flexbox's strength in single-row/column, content-driven layouts like a toolbar
Only when building a page with no responsive requirements
Grid and Flexbox are fully interchangeable with no tradeoffs
questions.explanation: Grid is suited to two-dimensional layout where rows and columns need to align; Flexbox suits one-dimensional arrangement, and real UIs often combine both.
